item.title: Episode 37: Busan, 2024: What Is Watching Mina Through Her Phone?
item.description:
In this original fiction set in Busan, South Korea, in 2024, why does Mina’s phone show a threat inside her own hallway?
At 1:17 a.m., Mina’s phone starts a horror clip she never touched. The hallway on screen is her own, and a black shape folds smaller whenever she blinks. Holding a brass desk lamp, she retreats toward the kitchen. Then the screen shows the shape beside her. As the corridor stretches and the exit slips away, a hollow knot of smoke begins pushing through the glass. What happens if she breaks the screen that brought it here?
The Signal Beneath the Screen is original horror fiction. Busan and 2024 are its imagined setting, not the place and date of a documented haunting. The story transforms the watched-apparition tension of The Turn of the Screw into a new screen-bound threat; it does not present an unverified online trend as fact.

item.title: Episode 36: Darwin, 1929: What Moves When Mara Looks Away?
item.description:
In this original fiction set in Darwin, Australia, in 1929, what crosses the doorway whenever Mara looks away?
At 12:17 a.m., Mara unlocks a coastal radio hut for a haunted property showing. A red thread reveals a doorway that should not exist. Through it comes the Ribbon Doll: cracked wood, one black ribbon eye, and a larger, inhuman silhouette of smoke. Every time Mara looks away, it crosses exactly one doorway, leaving a wet print where there is no water. By the third bell, her mapped exit is blocked. Can she close the threshold before the catalogue claims another item?

item.title: Episode 35: Kuldhara, 1825: Why Did the Shadows Leave Last?
item.description:
Why did a surveyor at Kuldhara near Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, India, count one extra shadow after the village's legendary 1825 abandonment?
Before Meera reaches the abandoned village, she hears a pencil moving inside her locked survey case. She has until dawn to finish the map her late father could not complete, and she refuses to leave the same grid unfinished. At Kuldhara’s gate, an old keeper gives her the field ledger and one instruction: count walls, not shadows.
The episode turns a routine night survey into an acoustic maze. Rafiq’s lantern hisses out. Wind drops away from the roofless houses. A pencil adds a forty-second line to a map that contains only forty-one buildings. Then moonlight reaches the lane from two directions, placing three shadows beneath two living people. Meera says the number aloud, and the extra shadow rises.
Listen closely as chalk numbers disappear from the doors and the iron gate becomes a featureless wall. The field ledger carries her father’s last message: a false mark is an empty house asking for a name. Meera can restore the exit, but Kuldhara will not open it for free. The final moments leave the horror behind in an ordinary survey office, where every chair casts a shadow except hers.
A restrained voice performance, scratching graphite, brittle paper, dying lantern flame, desert wind, shifting stone acoustics, and an original score build the episode’s dread for headphones. The tension comes from counting, silence, and the distance between a person and the shadow that should belong to her.
This story is fiction inspired by the legend of Kuldhara’s abandonment in 1825. Meera, Rafiq, the old keeper, the survey, House Forty-Two, and all supernatural events are invented. Historical reference: Rajasthan Tourism, “Kuldhara Village History: A Haunted Village near Jaisalmer.”

item.title: Episode 33: Paraná, 1947: Why Did the Grave Give Him Back?
item.description:
Why did a 1947 folklore geography place the earth-rejected Corpo-Seco in Paraná, Brazil, where even death refused him?
First comes the sound of disturbed earth. Then a coffin strikes the surface for the third time, and the villagers stop digging. Bento, keeper of the burial road, is handed a mule cart, a tin lantern, and one rule: whatever voice the thing inside steals, never answer it with a name. The road is supposed to carry Joaquim Vale’s rejected body until dawn. Bento’s feverish daughter Rosa, however, is waiting at home for the medicine in his coat.
This headphone-first folk-horror drama follows Bento through a chain of impossible refusals. A chapel bell rings while its rope hangs still. Coals die beneath cold ash. The cemetery itself shoves the coffin back onto the cart. When the mule bolts and the wheels continue in silence, a voice from behind the coffin lid calls him Father—while Rosa’s real cough answers from her window. Every sound pulls Bento closer to the one word the road needs.
Close voice performances, an unmoving bell, wooden wheels, coffin scratches, pine wind, black-dust textures, and an original score turn the burial road into an intimate acoustic trap. Listen for the contrast between the stolen voice inside the coffin and the fragile signs of Rosa beyond it; that distance carries the episode’s dread.
The story is fiction inspired by Brazilian Corpo-Seco traditions associated with Paraná through Luís da Câmara Cascudo’s folklore geography, first published in 1947. Joaquim Vale, Bento, Rosa, the burial road, the name trap, and all events in this episode are fictional.

item.title: Episode 30: The Doll That Asked Lucía to Take Its Place
item.description:
Before the first whisper, you will hear a lantern boat moving through black canal water and the night insects surrounding a lonely chinampa. Then the crickets vanish, a cord breaks, and a familiar voice calls from beneath the reeds.
Lucía has come to Mateo's island plot in Xochimilco with a clean doll to add to the hundreds already hanging from the ahuejote trees. Mateo is the caretaker, and every offering is meant to watch over him. One waterlogged doll obeys a different rule. It faces the canal, and Mateo warns Lucía that if it ever says Replace me, the words are not a request for cloth.

The tension comes from a single mistaken answer and the terrible difference between bringing a replacement and becoming one. The story is a fictional retelling inspired by reported accounts surrounding the Island of the Dolls in Xochimilco, Mexico City, where a caretaker began hanging dolls during the twentieth century. Lucía, Mateo, the copied voice, and the replacement bargain are fictional creations.
